In this lesson you will learn about troubleshooting electronic equipment using the AM receiver.
INTRODUCTIONM
In previous lessons you learned about troubleshooting individual circuits.
The method for troubleshooting equipment is similar to troubleshooting circuits.
The only difference in troubleshooting electronic equipment is that you must find which circuit is faulty.
The same troubleshooting skills required to repair an AM receiver are required to repair other electronic equipment no matter how complex.

TROUBLESHOOTING THEORY
The same skills that a technician uses to find a faulty circuit in an AM receiver are used to locate faulty circuits in all electronic circuits in all electronic equipment.

If you learn to approach all equipment failures with the same logical method, you will become a skilled electronic technician.
The method used to troubleshoot electronic equipment is similar to troubleshooting individual circuits.
TROUBLESHOOTING CHECKLIST
The only difference is that the steps must be expanded to include all the circuits in the equipment.
TROUBLESHOOTING CHECKLIST
Lets start with analyzing the equipment.
TROUBLESHOOTING CHECKLIST
You must first "know the equipment". You cannot tell if the equipment is faulty unless you know what it is supposed to do.
Then you must identify the symptom. That is, what is the problem.
This is referred to as symptom recognition. For example, this receiver has no output.
In more complex equipment, such as a TV, the problem could be one or more of the following:
>DFFGMNNOR
Be sure to identify ALL symptoms. This is called symptom elaboration. Each symptom gives clues to the faulty function and circuit.
The next step is to check the setup........................
TROUBLESHOOTING CHECKLIST
This is when you check all the controls, switches and connections to insure that they are in the proper position or configuration.
For example, if your symptom is no output, check that the receiver is turned on!
Also (and don't laugh because it is a common fault), check to see if the receiver is plugged in.
If the receiver is portable, check that the batteries are installed and that they are good.
The next step is to Calculate and Measure..................
TROUBLESHOOTING CHECKLIST
Until now, all the troubleshooting steps have been limited to controls, switches and connections.
Now test equipment is used to isolate the problem down to the faulty component.
The Calculate and Measure step is divided into three parts. This is the difference between troubleshooting circuits and electronic equipment.
First, determine the faulty function using a functional diagram and test equipment.
For example in an AM receiver, connect a known modulated RF signal to the tuner.
Then check the input and output signals of each functional block using an oscilloscope and compare to expected or calculated values.
The point where the input to a block is correct and output is incorrect identifies the faulty block.
The procedure to follow for identifying the faulty function is to start in the middle of the functional diagram.
If the signal is incorrect, the problem is before this point, in the tuner or IF amplifier.
If the signal is correct, the problem is after this point, in the detector or AF amplifier.
Continue halving the block diagram until the faulty circuit is isolated.
Once the faulty function has been isolated, use schematics and test equipment to determine the faulty circuit.
For example, there are three circuits in the AF amplifier block.
Use an oscilloscope to determine the faulty circuit by measuring the input and output signals of each circuit.
Start by measuring signals in the middle of the diagram.
If the signal at TP22 is correct, then the fault is in the audio push-pull amplifier circuit.
If the signal at TP22 is incorrect, then the fault is in the audio preamplifier or audio driver.
Measuring the signal at TP21 will isolate the fault to the circuit.
Once the faulty circuit is isolated, determine the faulty component.
Use an oscilloscope or multimeter and troubleshoot the circuit as a standard common emitter amplifier circuit.
The last step is to check results..........................
TROUBLESHOOTING CHECKLIST
Always check to see if the suspected faulty component can cause all the symptoms identified in step 1.
If so, replace the component and repeat step1 (analyze equipment) to ensure that the receiver is functioning correctly.
If the suspected faulty component can not cause the symptom, or all of the symptoms, further troubleshooting is required.
If the suspected component could not cause the symptom, repeat step 3, Calculate and measure.
If some of the symptoms still remain there is another fault present. Repair the first fault and repeat steps 1 through 4 for other faults.
Finding faulty components is easy no matter how complex the equipment is, if you use the four step troubleshooting method.

After connecting a known RF input into the tuner, you first measure the signal between the _______.
Measuring a correct signal at this point would indicate the fault is in the IF Amp, detector or AF Amp (tuner OK). This does not divide the receiver in half.
TRY AGAIN!
Measuring an incorrect signal at this point would indicate the fault is in the tuner, IF amp or detector (AF Amp OK). This does not divide the receiver in half.

If the signal between the IF Amp and detector is incorrect, what are the possible faulted functional blocks?
The input signal to the detector is incorrect. The detector will not function with an incorrect input. This will also cause the audio Amp. not to function correctly.
TRY AGAIN!
The IF amplifier may be faulted, its output signal is incorrect. However, the detector has an incorrect input and will not function correctly.
TRY AGAIN!
Between which two functional blocks would you measure next?
You already determined there is a fault in either the tuner or IF Amp. Measuring between the detector and audio Amp. would not help you isolate the fault.
TRY AGAIN!
If the signal between the tuner and IF amplifier is correct, what is the faulted block?
The output of the tuner is correct, the tuner function is working correctly.
TRY AGAIN!
Which test point in the IF amplifier circuits would be checked now?
TP9 is the input to the IF amplifiers. It has already been determined that this signal is correct. The output of the tuner was good.
TRY AGAIN!
TP17 is one of the outputs from the IF amplifiers. It has already been determined that this signal is incorrect.
Measuring the signal at TP12 indicates a correct signal. Which circuit is faulted??
The input signal to the second IF Amp. is correct. This indicates that the first IF Amp. is functioning correctly.
TRY AGAIN!

The base signals are normal, the fault is not in the base circuit of Q3.
TRY AGAIN!
The collector bias is normal, only the AC signal is low. With the proper input to the base, the collector circuit is not at fault.
What component in the emitter circuit would cause a low AC output on the collector?
If R10 was faulted, the emitter DC bias would be incorrect.
TRY AGAIN!
An open bypass capacitor would place an AC signal on the emitter causing the gain of Q3 to decrease.

The circuits for the AM receiver are contained on three PC cards, PC130-38, 39 and 40.
PC130-38 e faulty function, circuit and component.
PC130-39 e faulty function, circuit and component.

PC130-38 is the tuner section. It contains the RF amplifier, local oscillator and the mixer._
PC130-39 is the IF amplifier and detector. It contains the first and second IF amplifiers along with the detector.
PC130-40 is the audio amplifier. It contains an audio preamplifier, audio driver and audio push-pull amplifier.
